questions.q: When can you first inspect a parameter's gradient norm in a training step?
options: Before the forward pass runs
After loss.backward() has run and before optimizer.step()
Only after optimizer.step() has already updated the weights
Gradients cannot be inspected directly in PyTorch
questions.explain: backward() populates each trainable parameter's .grad tensor. That's the point in the loop where you can compute and inspect gradient norms, before the optimizer consumes them.

questions.q: What distinguishes the practical symptoms of vanishing gradients from exploding gradients?
options: Vanishing gradients always crash training immediately; exploding gradients never do
Vanishing gradients are quiet — loss just stalls with gradient norms near zero; exploding gradients are loud — loss spikes or goes to nan with huge gradient norms
They are the same phenomenon with different names
Vanishing gradients only occur in CNNs; exploding gradients only occur in RNNs
questions.explain: Vanishing gradients tend to be quiet: training appears stuck with near-zero gradient norms, without anything crashing. Exploding gradients are typically loud, producing loss spikes or nan/inf values that are hard to miss.

options: It deletes any gradient larger than 1.0
It rescales the model's gradients in place so their combined norm does not exceed max_norm, and returns the pre-clipping total norm
It resets all gradients to zero
It changes the learning rate to 1.0 for that step
questions.explain: clip_grad_norm_ computes the total gradient norm, and if it exceeds max_norm, rescales all gradients proportionally so the combined norm equals max_norm. It returns the norm as it was before any clipping was applied.

questions.q: In a deep network experiencing vanishing gradients, what pattern would you typically see when printing grad_norm per layer?
options: All layers show identical, stable gradient norms
Only the output layer has a nonzero gradient
Early layers often show gradient norms orders of magnitude smaller than later layers
Gradient norms are unrelated to layer depth
questions.explain: Because each layer's backward pass multiplies by another factor that can shrink the gradient signal, early layers in a deep network frequently end up with much smaller gradient norms than the later layers closer to the loss.

questions.q: Why is logging the return value of clip_grad_norm_ useful, rather than just calling it and ignoring the result?
options: It has no useful meaning and can be safely discarded
It reports the GPU memory freed by clipping
A pre-clipping norm that's frequently much larger than max_norm tells you clipping is actively doing real work, not just acting as an unused safeguard
It reports the post-clipping norm, confirming the clip succeeded
questions.explain: clip_grad_norm_ returns the total norm as computed before clipping. Tracking this over training reveals how often and how aggressively clipping is intervening — valuable diagnostic signal, not just a formality.
